translations.text: In the twelfth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, who reigned over the Assyrians in the great city of Nineveh, in the days of Arphaxad, who reigned over the Medes in the region of Ecbatana,
he built a city there and surrounded Ecbatana with walls of dressed stones, three cubits wide and six cubits long, and made the wall seventy cubits high.
He established its towers on foundations on either side of the gates, a hundred cubits in length, and made their width sixty cubits at the foundation.
And he also made its gates seventy cubits high and forty cubits wide, for the passage of the forces of the commanders of his army and for the ordered ranks of his infantry.
In those days King Nebuchadnezzar made war against King Arphaxad on the great plain in the territory of Ragau.

The inhabitants of the hill country gathered and assembled with him, along with all who lived along the Euphrates, the Tigris, and the Hydaspes River, and on the plain of Arioch, king of the Elymeans. Very many nations gathered to wage war against the sons of Chelod.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, sent word to the inhabitants of Persia and to the inhabitants of the western regions: the inhabitants of Cilicia, Damascus, and Lebanon, and all the inhabitants who lived facing the seacoast,
and those who belonged to the people of Carmel, and Gilead, Upper Galilee, and the great plain of Jezreel,
and all Samaria and those who were in its cities, and beyond the Jordan River as far as Jerusalem, Betane, Chellus, Kadesh, the river of Egypt, Tahpanhes, and Rameses,
and all the land of Goshen as far as Memphis and Tanis, and all the inhabitants of Egypt as far as the borders of Ethiopia.

But all the inhabitants of the land insolently rejected the words of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, and did not agree to go with him to war, because they were not afraid of him. His messengers were treated as worthless and greatly dishonored in their sight.

Nebuchadnezzar became very angry with the land and swore by his kingdom and his throne, saying, “I will take vengeance on the mountains of Cilicia and on the people of Damascus and Syria, and destroy them all with my sword—the inhabitants of Moab, the sons of Ammon, all Judea, and all the Egyptians, as far as the boundaries of the two seas.”

He prepared and drew up his entire army against King Arphaxad in the seventeenth year. He prevailed in his war and brought under his control all the forces of Arphaxad, all their horses, and all their weapons and chariots.
He took possession of his cities. He advanced as far as Ecbatana and captured its towers, demolished and plundered its public squares, and turned its splendor into a disgrace.
And he captured Arphaxad in the territory of Rhagae and killed him with his own sword.
He brought back his troops, who had come with him from the foreign nations, a very great multitude. He and all his troops remained there in ease and merriment for a hundred and twenty days.
In the eighteenth year, on the twelfth day of the first month, he reviewed his troops and consulted with them about taking vengeance on the whole land.
He summoned all his nobles and his governors,
and told them the plans he intended to carry out. From his own mouth, in the hearing of the troops, he set out in full all the harm to be done to the land.
They answered, saying, “Let everyone who opposes the king be destroyed, and anyone who does not obey the word of his commands.”

When he had finished these deliberations, Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, summoned Holofernes, the commander of all his armies, and said to him, “Thus says the great king, lord over all this earth: You shall go out from my presence and choose to take with you men who trust in their strength: one hundred and twenty thousand infantry and a very large force of one hundred and twenty thousand cavalry. You shall march against the western region, because they have disobeyed the words of my commands. You shall command them to prepare earth and water, for I will march against them in my anger, cover the face of the whole earth, and trample it underfoot with my might. I will hand them over to all my armies to plunder. Their wounded shall fill their valleys and ravines, and their rivers shall flow with their blood. I will bring captivity upon them from the ends of the earth. You shall go out, surround their territories, and besiege them for me. Then they shall surrender themselves to you, and you shall keep them for me until the day of their distress and punishment.

My eye shall not spare those who have disobeyed me, but shall give them over to death and plunder throughout all your land. For as I live, I have spoken by the power of my kingdom, and I will carry out all my wishes. You must not disregard even one word of the command I have given you. Instead, carry out everything completely, just as I have told you, and do not delay in doing this.”

Holofernes left his lord’s presence and summoned all the princes and commanders of the Assyrians. From among them he selected and counted out men for battle, as his lord had commanded him: one hundred and twenty thousand men, and one hundred and twenty thousand mounted archers.

He organized and equipped them in battle formation. He took a great many camels and pack animals to carry the equipment and supplies, and sheep, cattle, and herds of goats for their provisions, beyond counting,
and gave them all provisions for the journey,
and a very great quantity of gold and silver from the king’s house.

He and all the army with him set out for war, to prepare for the king to go out and cover the face of the whole western land with weapons, chariots, horses, and carefully selected infantry. Others who had joined them were like a multitude of locusts and like the sand of the earth, for their multitude could not be counted.

They traveled from the city of Nineveh for three days to the plain of Bectileth and camped near the mountain, to the left of Upper Cilicia. He took his whole army—the cavalry, the infantry, the weapons, and the chariots—and went from there into the hill country,
and struck Put and Lud. He destroyed and plundered all the descendants of Rasses and Ishmael who lived along the edge of the wilderness south of Chelleon.
He crossed the Euphrates River and traveled through Mesopotamia. He attacked and defeated all the fortified cities along the valley of Nabora, as far as the borders of the sea,
and reached and occupied the territory of the Cilicians, striking down and destroying everyone who opposed him. He came as far as the southern borders of Japheth, opposite Arabia.
And he confined and imprisoned all the descendants of Midian, burned all their houses and tents, and demolished and destroyed all their livestock pens.

And he went down to the plain of Damascus during the wheat harvest and burned all their fields and farms. He destroyed their flocks and herds, plundered their cities, slaughtered their children, and struck down and killed their young men with the sword.

Dread and fear fell upon the inhabitants of the seacoast, of Tyre and Sidon, upon the inhabitants of Syria and Iucina, and upon all the inhabitants of Jamnia. Those who lived in Azotus and Ashkelon were greatly afraid of him.
They sent messengers to him to speak with him in words of peace, saying:
Look, we are servants of Nebuchadnezzar, and we stand before you. Do with us whatever seems pleasing to you.

For here are our houses, all our wheat fields, our flocks and herds, and all the enclosures for our livestock before your eyes. Do whatever seems good to you. Our towns and their inhabitants are your servants. Come and enter them as seems good to you.
The messengers came to Holofernes and reported these words to him.
He himself went down to the coast with his army and stationed guards in the towns on the heights. From those towns he took chosen men to fight alongside him.
Those towns came out to meet him
with songs, wreaths, cymbals, and drums.
He dug up their boundaries and removed all their woodland.
He had been commanded to destroy the gods of the land,
so that all nations would worship Nebuchadnezzar alone and the peoples would call him God.
He came opposite Esdraelon, which was near the inhabitants, opposite the great mountain of Judea.
He camped between Geba and Beth-shan and remained there for a month, gathering rations and provisions for his troops.

When the Israelites and the inhabitants of Judea heard what Holofernes and the commanders of the king of the Assyrians had done to the nations and the Gentiles, and how he had demolished all their temples and brought them to ruin,

they were greatly afraid of him and were troubled about Jerusalem and the house of their God. For at that time they had returned from their captivity and had only recently gathered in Judea, and they had just purified the altar of the Lord their God, its vessels, and the house from their defilement.
They sent word throughout all the territory of Samaria, to Kona-Beth-horon, Belmaim, Jericho, Choba, Soumain, and the valleys of Salem.
They went and occupied all the high mountain summits, fortified the villages on them, and prepared and stored provisions there for warfare, for their fields had been harvested at that time.
And Joakim, the high priest who was in Jerusalem in those days, wrote to the inhabitants of Bethulia and Betomestha, which is opposite Esdraelon, facing the plain near Dothan.

And he said, “Go and seize the passes of the hill country, for these were the entrances into Judea. It was easy for them to block the enemy, because the passes through the gorges were narrow enough for two men to guard.”
The Israelites did as Joakim the high priest and the council of elders of the people of Israel, who sat in Jerusalem, had commanded them.
Every man of Israel cried out to the Lord with all their heart, and they humbled themselves, both they and their wives.
All the foreigners and hired workers, together with their livestock, [?], and their slaves bought with silver put sackcloth around their waists.

Every man of Israel, with their wives and children who lived in Jerusalem, fell down before the temple of the Lord and pleaded. They put ashes on their heads, shook out their sackcloth before the Lord, and draped sackcloth over the altars of the sanctuary. Together they cried out to the God of Israel with all their heart, asking him not to hand their children over to be seized as spoil, their wives to plunder, the towns of their inheritance to destruction, or the sanctuary to defilement, disgrace, and the mockery of the Gentiles. The Lord heard their voice and saw their afflictions. The people continued fasting throughout Judea and in Jerusalem before the sanctuary of the Lord Almighty.

Joakim the high priest and all the priests and ministers of the Lord who stood before the Lord were clothed in sackcloth. They offered the regular burnt offerings, the prayers, the freewill offerings, and the sacrifices of the people.
There were ashes on the cloths covering their heads, and they cried out to the Lord with all their hearts to visit the house of Israel and do good to it.

They reported to Holofernes, the commander of the Assyrian army, that the Israelites had prepared for war, blocked the passes through the mountain regions, fortified all the high mountain summits, and hidden traps in the plains.
Holofernes became furious, burning with great anger, and summoned all the rulers of Moab, the commanders of Ammon, and all the nobles of the coastal region.

And he said to them, “Tell me, you descendants of Canaan: who are these people who live in the hill country? What are the cities in which they live? How numerous are their forces? What is the source of their strength and power? Who is their king and the leader of their army?”
“Why have they turned their minds aside and refused to come out to meet me, acting more arrogantly than all the inhabitants of the west?”

Achior, the leader of all the Ammonites, said to him, “Let my lord hear the words of your servant, and I will tell you the truth about this people who live in that mountain region near you. No falsehood will come from your servant’s mouth.
These people are descended from the Chaldeans.
They first lived as foreigners in Mesopotamia because they did not wish to worship the gods of their ancestors in the land of the Chaldeans.

They left their ancestral land and worshiped the God of heaven, whom they had come to know as the true God. They went to Mesopotamia and lived there as foreigners for many days. Their God told them to leave the place where they lived as foreigners and come to the land of Canaan. They settled there and became rich in gold, silver, and many livestock.

They went down to Egypt because there was a famine in the land of the Canaanites. They lived there as foreigners until they had grown numerous. They became exceedingly many there, and their people could not be counted.
The king of the Egyptians rose against them, tormenting them with suffering and brickwork, and they were forced into slavery.
They cried out to their God, and he struck the land of the Egyptians with incurable plagues. The Egyptians drove them out of their presence.
And God dried up the Red Sea before them.
He led them along the way to Sinai and Kadesh-barnea, and they drove out all the inhabitants of the wilderness.
They established settlements in the land of the Amorites and destroyed all the people of Heshbon by their own strength. They crossed the Jordan and took possession of the whole land.
They drove out from their presence the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, Shechem, and all the Girgashites, and they lived in the land for many days.
As long as they did not sin before their God, every good thing was with them, because the God who hates injustice was with them.

But when they rejected the ways of God’s covenant, they were destroyed in very many battles and were taken captive to a foreign land that was not their own. The temple of their God was ruined, and their cities were handed over to their enemies.

Now they have returned to the Lord their God and have gathered from their captivity, where they had been scattered. They have taken possession of the city of Jerusalem, where the sanctuary was, and have settled in the mountain region, for it was desolate.

So now, my lord, if there is some act of ignorance among their people and they sin against their God, let us watch and wait for this, because it will be their stumbling block. Then let us assemble against them and wage war on them.
But if they have committed no injustice against their God, let us pass them by, my lord, lest the Lord their God defend them and we become an object of shame and reproach throughout the earth.”
And when Achior had finished speaking these words, the whole army around the tent began to grumble.
The officers, the inhabitants of the coastal regions, and the Moabites told Holofernes to punish Achior: “For we have no fear of the Israelites, a people who have no strength for warfare.
Now let us go out, and let them become food for all your troops, Lord Holofernes.”

When those around their tent had finished speaking, Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army, said to Achior before all the foreign troops: “Who are you, Achior, to stand against all the foreign peoples and the Moabites and the mercenaries from Ephraim,

that you have prophesied to us as you have today, saying that we should not wage war against the Israelites because their God protects them? And who is God except Nebuchadnezzar? He will send his forces and destroy them from the earth, and their God will not rescue them.

But we, his servants, will drive them back as though they were one man. They will not be able to stand against our mounted cavalry. We will wipe them out with them, drench their mountains with their blood, and fill their plains with their corpses. They will no longer be able to stand before us, but will utterly perish,
says King Nebuchadnezzar, lord of all the earth, for he has spoken, and the words of his mouth have not proved empty.

But you, Achior, mercenary of Ammon, have spoken these words in your wickedness. From this day onward you will not see my face again until I take vengeance on the nation that came out of Egypt. Then the sword of my troops will pass through your sides.”

“And you will fall among the many wounded when I return. But now my servants will take you back to the hill country and leave you at the passes of a city that lies along the routes through them. You will not perish until you are destroyed together with them. And if you hope in your heart that they will not be handed over to this fate, do not be confident, for I have spoken, and not one of my words will fail.”
And Holofernes ordered his servants who stood before him to bind Achior, take him to Bethulia, and hand him over to the Israelites.

His servants seized him and brought him outside the camp into the plain. They went from the plain and came to the mountainside by the springs below Bethulia, which is in Samaria. When the men of the city saw them on the mountaintop, they took their weapons and rushed against them on the mountaintop. All the slingers blocked their ascent and hurled stones at them.
They went along the foot of the mountain, bound Achior, and left him at the foot of the mountain. Then they went back to their lord.
The Israelites came down from the city, reached him, untied him, and brought him to Bethulia. They placed him before the rulers of their city,
who in those days were Uzziah son of Micah, of the tribe of Simeon, and Carmi son of Elchiel.

They gathered all the elders of the city, all the young men, and all the women into the assembly, and summoned Achior into the midst of all the people. Uzziah asked him, “Why has this happened to you?” He answered and recounted the words spoken in Holofernes’ council and everything he himself had said among the officers of the Assyrians,
and everything Holofernes had said boastfully about the house of Israel.
And all the people of the land fell to their knees and worshiped God, crying out and saying,
“Lord God of heaven, look upon their arrogance and have mercy on the lowly condition of our nation. Look upon your sanctuary, Lord, in these days.”
And they prayed. They comforted Achior and praised him greatly.
And Uzziah took him from the assembly and brought him to his house.
And he held a feast for him with the elders and priests. Throughout that whole night they cried out to the Lord, the God of Israel.
The next morning Holofernes gave orders to his troops, and those who had come to help him gathered to march against Bethulia, occupy the mountain passes, and wage war against the Israelites.

They equipped themselves and made ready, and that day all the fighting men marched out: the infantry numbered one hundred and seventy thousand, and the armed cavalry twelve thousand, besides all the other common people and a very great quantity of baggage and equipment.

They camped in the valley near Bethulia, beside the spring. They extended the front of their camp southward, across to Dothaim and Belbaim, and lengthwise from Bethulia to Cyamon, which faces Esdraelon—that is, Jezreel.

When the Israelites saw such a great multitude, they were deeply alarmed and said to one another, “Now they will lick up the whole face of the earth. Neither the high mountains nor the valleys and hills will be able to withstand their strength.”
Each of the Israelites took up his weapons. They lit torches on the city’s towers and stood guard throughout that whole night.

On the second day Holofernes brought out all his cavalry before the Israelites who were in Bethulia. He reached the approaches to their city, inspected the springs of water, and hastened to besiege them. He stationed companies of fighting men against them, while he himself went back to his camp.
Then all the Ammonites, all the assemblies and leaders of the Moabites, and the commanders of the coastal peoples approached him and said:

“Let our lord listen to the words of his servants, so that your troops may suffer no losses. These Israelites do not trust in their spears or their weapons, but in the high mountains where they live, which cannot even be reached. Now, lord, do not engage them in open battle, as warfare is ordinarily conducted, and not a single man of your army will fall. Instead, keep still and remain in your camp, and you will preserve your troops. Let your servants seize the springs of water that flow from the foot of the mountain, for all the inhabitants of that city drink from there. They will perish from thirst and then hand the city over to you themselves. With all our commanders we will go up onto the nearby high mountains and camp upon them as one man. They themselves, their wives, and their children will waste away from hunger and thirst. Before the sword reaches them, they will fall dead in the streets of their city. Thus you will repay them for their wickedness, because they resisted you in battle and did not submit to you peacefully.”

The plan pleased Holofernes and all his servants, and he ordered them to do as they had proposed. The army of the Ammonites went out, accompanied by five thousand Assyrians, and they camped in the valley. They came and seized the Israelites’ springs of water. The descendants of Esau and the Ammonites went up and camped along the mountainside opposite Dothan. They sent some of their men southward and northward, opposite Egrebel, which is near Chus, above the valley of Cumur. The rest of the Assyrian forces camped in the plain and covered the whole face of the land. The other common people, with their equipment, possessions, and tents, also camped there in very great numbers. The Israelites cried out to the Lord their God, for terror had struck them and their spirits were exhausted. Their enemies had surrounded and besieged them, and they had no way to escape from among them. The Assyrian forces remained and besieged them with their weapons, chariots, and horses for thirty-four days.

All the inhabitants of Bethulia became weak and exhausted. All their containers were empty of water, and their cisterns were drained dry. There was not enough to drink for even one day, and whatever they drank was measured and weighed out.

Their women and children were distressed and bewildered. Their young men were exhausted from thirst and lay collapsed in the city squares and the passageways of the gates, with no relief from anywhere. All the people gathered against Uzziah and the rulers of the city—young men, women, and children. They wept loudly and said before all the elders of the people:
“May God judge between us and you, because you have wronged us by not negotiating peace with the Assyrians.
Now there is no one to help us. Instead, God has handed us over to them, so that we fall stricken before them and perish from terrible thirst.
So now appeal to them and hand over this whole city to them as plunder.
It is better for us to become their captives and slaves and remain alive, because we cannot bear to see the children and women die before our own eyes, as their spirits fail and are exhausted.

Now we call heaven and earth and the God of our fathers to witness against you—the God who exacts retribution from us according to the sins of our fathers—so that he may not act according to these words in these days.”
There was great weeping and mourning throughout the whole assembly, and together they cried out loudly to the Lord God.
Uzziah said to them, “Take courage, brothers, and endure for five more days. During that time the Lord will send his mercy upon us,
for he will not abandon us completely.

If these days pass and no help comes to us, I will do as you have said.” Then he dismissed the people to their homes and to the towers and walls of the city to keep watch against the enemy. They remained distressed and deeply bewildered.

On that day Judith heard about this. She was the daughter of Merari, son of Ox, son of Joseph, son of Uzziel, son of Elkiah, son of Elijah, son of Hilkiah, son of Eliab, son of Nathanael, son of Samamiel, son of Sarasadai, son of Israel.
Her husband, Manasseh, was of her own clan and family. Her husband died during the barley harvest.

For he was overseeing his reapers in the field when the scorching wind swept over him and struck his head. Because of this he died in Bethulia, his own city, and was buried with his ancestors on the estate near Dothan and Balson.
Judith lived as a widow in her house for three years and four months.
She made a shelter on the roof of her house, put sackcloth around her waist, and wore the clothing of widowhood.
She fasted throughout her widowhood, except on the Sabbath, the new moons, the annual festivals, and the joyful occasions of the house of Israel.
She was very beautiful to look at. Her husband Manasseh had left her gold and silver, male and female servants, fields, estates, and livestock, and Judith herself managed these.
And no one said anything evil about her, for she feared the Lord greatly.

When she heard what the people had wickedly said to the ruler because they were exhausted by thirst, Judith also heard the words Uzziah had spoken to the people and how he had promised them that after five days he would hand the city over to the Assyrians. She sent her maid, who was in charge of all her possessions, and summoned Uzziah, Chabris, Charmis, and all the elders of her city.

They came to her, and she said to them, “Listen to me, inhabitants of Bethulia. The words you have spoken before the people in these days are not right. You confirmed with an oath what you said before God in your midst, declaring that you would hand this city over to our enemies if the Lord did not send us help.
And now, you who are putting God to the test in these days—this now stands established among human beings.
Look, you do not now consult the Lord Almighty, and you know nothing.

For the depth of a human heart cannot be discovered, and you cannot comprehend the thoughts of their hearts. How, then, could you examine God, who made all these things, know his wishes, or look into his counsels? Far be it from you, brothers! Do not provoke the Lord our God.
If he does not wish to help us within five days, he has the power to protect us whenever he wishes, at any time, or to destroy us before our enemies.
But do not bind the plans of the Lord your God to yourselves, for God's threats are not like a man's, nor does he punish like a human being.
“But now let us wait in expectation of receiving mercy from him. Let us plead with him and call upon him to help us, and he will hear the voice of our prayers if it pleases him.”

For no such thing has ever arisen among our nation, nor has anything like it existed to this day in our nation, our tribe, our people, or our cities. They do not bow down to things made by human hands,
as happened in former days. Because of this, our ancestors were handed over to the sword and to plunder, and suffered great destruction before their enemies.
But we have known no other God besides him, in whom we hope that he will not disregard us

and will not hand over our nation in this way, as you have pledged, or plunder our sanctuary. Or will he not exact vengeance for the enemies’ insults against the sanctuary and bring the death of our brothers, the captivity of this land, and the devastation of our inheritance back upon our heads among all the nations where we will serve them? We will become objects of shame and reproach before those who possess us. For our slavery to them will not turn out joyfully; rather, the Lord our God will make us an object of dishonor and ruin to them.”

And now, brothers, let us show our brothers that their lives depend on us, and that the holy things, the altar, and the temple stand secure through us. And now, for all this, give thanks to our God, who tests us as he tested our fathers.
Remember how much he did to Abraham, and how he dealt with Isaac and with Jacob in Mesopotamia of the Syrians, when he tended the flocks of Laban, his mother's brother.

For he has not tested us as he tested them to discover the thoughts of their hearts, nor will he call our sins to account. Rather, the Lord afflicts those who are close to him to discipline and teach them.

And Uzziah said to her, “Everything you have said, you have spoken from the fullness of your heart and with good judgment, and no one can oppose your words. For your wisdom has not become apparent only today: from earlier days all the people have known your understanding, because the inclinations of your heart are good. But the people were very thirsty, and we were compelled to do as we told them and to take upon ourselves an oath that we cannot break.
Now, plead with God in prayer, for you are a righteous woman, and the Lord will send rain, and these cisterns will be filled, and we will no longer be in need.”
And Judith said to them, “Listen to me, and I will do something that will be told to generations after generations and to children after children.

Stand at the gate of this city tonight, and I will go out with my maid. Within these days in which you have pledged to surrender this city into the hands of our enemies, the Lord God will come to our aid through my hand.
But do not inquire into what I am going to do, for I will not tell you until what I am doing is accomplished.”

And Uzziah, together with the leaders, said to her, “Go in peace, and may the Lord God of Israel be with you to exact vengeance on our enemies.” And they returned from Judith's tent, each to his own post guarding the walls.

And Judith fell on her face, took off the sackcloth she was wearing, and scattered ashes on her head. At that same hour the evening incense was being offered in Jerusalem in the temple of the Lord. She cried out loudly to the Lord God, and Judith said:
“Lord, God of my father Simeon, into whose hand you put a sword to exact vengeance on the foreigners

who violated a virgin's womb to defile her, stripped her limbs bare to shame her, and disgraced her virginity to dishonor her—things that were not pleasing in your sight. Therefore you handed their rulers over to bloodshed, together with the beds on which they were condemned, and destroyed the servants together with their masters, and the fathers upon their thrones. You gave their wives as plunder, their daughters into captivity, and all their spoils as portions to your beloved sons, who were zealous with your zeal, regarded the defilement of their sister as an abomination, and called upon you for help. And now, Lord my God, hear the voice of your maidservant and look upon the prayers of this widow.

For you did those things among them before, and those after them, and those of the present; and you planned the things that are to come. What happened was as you wished, and they appeared before you as you had planned.
And they said, ‘Here we are,’ for all your ways are prepared, and your judgments are made with foreknowledge.

For look, the Assyrian has filled this land with his forces. They have exalted themselves with their mounted horsemen and arrogantly boasted of the strength of their many infantrymen. They have trusted in spears, armor, and the skill of archers and slingers, and have not known that you are the Lord who crushes wars, and that Lord is your name. Save us from this distress.

Scatter their forces, Lord Almighty, and crush and overthrow their strength in your anger, for they have wished to defile your holy places and the dwelling of your name and glory, and to demolish the horns of your holy altar with iron.
Look and see their arrogance, and send your anger upon their heads. Give strength to the hand of your servant, this widow, to do what I have planned.
Strike down and overthrow the servant through the deception of my lips, and the ruler together with his servants, and crush their ferocity through the hand of this woman.

For your strength does not depend on numbers, nor does your authority rest with the mighty. Rather, you are the Lord God of the humble, the helper of the needy, the refuge of the weak, the defender of the destitute, and the savior of those without hope.
Yes, God of my father and God of Israel's inheritance, Lord of heaven and earth, creator of the waters, you are the king of all your creatures.

Hear the prayers of your servant. Give me words to speak for the overthrow of those who have come against your covenants, against your house and the heights of Zion, and against the dwelling of your children, for they have devised cruel plans.

Make your mighty arm known to your inheritance, so that they may know that you are God, who rules over all powers and authorities, for there is no one to protect this nation of Israel except you, Lord.
When Judith had finished her prayers and completed these words, she rose to her feet from lying bowed with her face to the ground.
She called her maid and went down into her house, where she observed the Sabbaths and feast days.

She took off the sackcloth she had been wearing and removed her widow's clothing. She washed her body with water, anointed herself with fragrant oil, braided the hair of her head, and tied a headdress around her forehead. She put on the festive clothes she used to wear while her husband Manasseh was alive.

And she put on gilded shoes, placed bracelets on her wrists, necklaces of precious stones inlaid with pearls around her neck, rings on her fingers, and [?] on her head. She arranged and adorned herself with all her ornaments and made herself exceedingly radiant, to deceive and beguile everyone who saw her with the beauty of her face.

She gave her maid a bag and filled it with roasted grain, cakes, and ritually pure bread, along with a container of wine and a flask of oil. She purified and prepared everything according to their law and gave it to her maid.
They went out through the gate of the city of Bethulia and saw Uzziah there, standing at the gate, with the other priests of the city, including Chabris and Charmis.
When they saw Judith, whose appearance and clothing had changed, they were greatly amazed at her beauty.

They said to her, “May God, the God of our fathers, grant you favor and fulfill the desires of your heart, for the gladness and joy of the children of Israel and for the good of Jerusalem.” And they bowed down before God.

Judith said to them, “Order the gates of this city to be opened for me, so that I may go out and carry out what you have discussed with me.” They ordered the gatekeepers to open them, as she had requested, and they did so.

And Judith herself went out, with her maid accompanying her. The men of the city watched her as she went, until she reached the foot of the mountain and passed through the gorge of the valley. Then they could no longer see her.
They went through the ravine of the valley, straight along the road, and the Assyrian guards met them.

They seized them, questioned her, and said, “To whom do you belong? Where do you come from, and where are you going?” Judith said to them, “I am a daughter of the Hebrews, and I have fled from them, because they are about to be handed over to you as food.

I have come to stand before Holofernes, the commander of your forces, to tell him the truth and show him the route by which he can go and take possession of the entire hill country, without a single man of his forces suffering harm.”
When the men heard Judith’s words, they looked at her face, and her beauty seemed very great to them. They said to her,
“You have saved your life today. Now hurry down to see our lord. Come with us to his tent, and we will hand you over to him.

When you stand before him, do not be afraid in your heart. Tell him what you have told us, and he will treat you well.” They selected a hundred men from among themselves and sent them with her. They brought them to Holofernes’ tent. They reported her beauty and her arrival throughout the whole camp, and people came to see her while she stood outside Holofernes’ tent, as they were reporting to Holofernes.
They were greatly amazed at her beauty and at all the Israelites.

Each man said to his companion, “Who can think anything evil against this nation, whose women have such beauty? Yet their men must not be allowed to live, so that their daughters may become our wives, for if they live, they will be a danger to the whole earth.” Holofernes’ attendants and all his servants came out and took her into the tent.

Holofernes was sitting on his throne, enclosed on every side by curtains embroidered with gold, pearls, and precious stones. When he heard about Judith, he came out into the entrance hall of the tent with torches and silver lamps, because it was night.
When Holofernes saw her, he was amazed at the sight of her beauty. Judith fell down and bowed before Holofernes, and his servants raised her up.
Holofernes said to her, “Take courage, woman, and do not be afraid, for I do not mistreat anyone who wishes to serve King Nebuchadnezzar, who rules this whole earth.
“And now, if your people who live in the hill country had not rebelled against me, I would not have raised my spear against them. But they themselves have brought this upon themselves.”

Now tell me why you have fled from them and come to us. Take courage, for you have come to safety. You will remain alive tonight and throughout all your days. No one will harm you, but you will be treated well, as are the servants of my lord Nebuchadnezzar.”

Judith said to him, “Receive the words of your servant, and let your servant speak before you. I will tell my lord no lie tonight. If you follow and listen to the words of your servant, God will accomplish a perfect work through you, and your word will not come to nothing.

For as surely as Nebuchadnezzar, king of the whole earth, lives, and as surely as his power lives—the power of the one who sent you to set all people in order—not only will people serve him through you, but also wild beasts, livestock, and the birds of heaven will live through you for Nebuchadnezzar and his whole household.

For we have heard of your wisdom and understanding. Indeed, it has been reported throughout the whole earth that you alone are a benefactor in all his kingdom, that you are powerful in speech and remarkable among the fighting forces.”

Now we too have heard the words that Achior spoke in your council chamber, and that the men of Bethulia spared him. He reported everything just as he had spoken to you. So now, my lord, do not disregard his words, but hold them firmly in your heart, for they are true.
For no one can afflict our nation, and no enemy’s sword can harm us, unless they sin against their God.

And now, my lord, neither you nor your army will suffer harm, for the time of their death has already come because of the sins they committed against their God, for they have committed a great sin of lawlessness.
For their water and food have run short.
They made plans and laid their hands on animals that their God had not permitted them to eat.

And they began eating the grain and the tithes of wine and oil that had been consecrated for the priests who minister in Jerusalem before our God—things that it was lawful only for the priests to eat, not for them. They sent to Jerusalem so that those who were there would do the same, for which they would receive forgiveness from God through the priests. And now that they have committed these sins, they are handed over to destruction.
Now I, your servant, fled from them when I learned of this. And he sent me to accomplish with you a great deed that will astonish everyone throughout the earth who hears of it.

For your servant worships God, and night and day I pray to the Lord, the God of heaven. Now I will remain with you, my lord, and your servant will go out at night into the ravine of the valley. I will stand in prayer before the Lord my God, and he will tell me when they sin against him.

Then I will come and tell you, and you will go out with your entire army, and none of them will escape you. I will lead you through Judea until I bring you to Jerusalem. You will set your throne in its midst and gather them like a flock without a shepherd, and not even a dog will bark at you. God has told me that this will happen, and I have come to make it known to you.
Her words pleased Holofernes and all his servants. They marveled at her wisdom and said:
“From one end of the earth to the other, no beautiful woman can be found who compares with her in wise speech and beauty of face.”

Holofernes said to her, “God has done well to send you to lead this people, so that our dominion may be strengthened and those who have rebelled against us may perish. Now I see that you are lovely in appearance, and all your words are good.”
“For if your God does as you have said, he will also be my God, and you will live in the house of Nebuchadnezzar and be renowned throughout the whole earth.”
He ordered her to be taken to the treasury house and commanded that she be given a portion of his own delicacies and some of the wine he himself drank.
Judith said, “I will not eat any of these things, lest they cause me to stumble. Instead, give me permission to eat what was brought for me from the city.”
Holofernes said to her, “If that runs out, where shall we get similar food to give you? For there is no one from your nation with us.”

Judith said to him, “As you live, my lord, your servant will not use up the food that came with me before he accomplishes through me what he has spoken.” Holofernes’ servants brought her into the tent, and she slept there until midnight. Judith rose during the morning watch.
And she sent word to Holofernes, saying, “Let my lord command that his maidservant be allowed to go out and pray.”
Holofernes ordered the guards not to prevent her from going out. She remained in the camp for three days.
She would go out at night into the valley of Bethulia and bathe at the springs of water there in the camp, according to Jewish law.
And while she bathed, she prayed to the Lord God of Israel to make her journey successful for the salvation of the children of her people.
And she would enter purified and remain in the tent until she fetched her food for herself in the evening.

On the fourth day, Holofernes held a banquet for his servants alone and invited no outsiders to the banquet. He said to Bagoas, his eunuch, who was the trusted chief officer over all his possessions, “Go and persuade the Hebrew woman who is with you to eat and drink with us.”
“What a disgrace and a mockery it would be for us to let such a woman go without speaking to her at all! If we do not take this woman and bring her close to us, she may make a laughingstock of us.”

Bagoas left Holofernes and went in to her and said, “Do not hesitate, beautiful servant girl, to come to my lord, to be honored by him, and to drink the wine of joy with him and with us. Today you will be like one of the daughters of the Assyrians who serve King Nebuchadnezzar.”
Judith said to him, “Who am I to refuse my lord?”
“For I will eagerly do everything that is pleasing in your eyes, and it will be a joy to me until the day of my death.”

She rose and adorned herself with her ornaments, as women adorn themselves. Her maid came forward and placed a seat for her on the ground opposite Holofernes—the leather cushion that she had received from Bagoas for her daily use—and Judith sat on it.
Holofernes became infatuated with her appearance, and his soul was stirred. He greatly desired to be with her, and Holofernes had been seeking to seduce her from the day he first saw her.
Holofernes said to her, “Drink and be merry with us.” Judith said, “Yes, my lord, for today my life has become greater than on any day since my birth.”
She took and ate and drank before him what her servant girl had prepared for her.
Holofernes was delighted with her and drank an exceedingly great amount of wine, more than he had ever drunk in his life since the day of his birth.
When evening came, he hurried his servants out, and Bagoas closed the doors of the tent. They each went to their own beds outside the tent.
For they were all weary and exhausted from drinking so much wine.
Judith and Holofernes remained alone in the tent.
Holofernes went to his bed and fell asleep, deeply stupefied by the wine.

Judith told her servant girl to stand outside the tent and wait for her when she came out, as on the other days. She had told her, “I am going to pray as usual,” and she had spoken to Bagoas in the same terms.

Everyone left the chamber, and no one at all remained there. Judith stood beside his bed and said, “Lord God of hosts, look at this hour upon the work of my hands and upon the exaltation of Jerusalem.”
“For now is the time for you to visit your inheritance and to accomplish this deed through my hands, for the destruction of our enemies who have risen against us.”
She approached the bedpost by Holofernes’ head and drew his dagger from his thigh.
She took hold of his hair and said, “Strengthen me, God of Israel, on this day.”
She struck his neck twice with all her strength, cut off his head, and lifted it away.
She rolled his body off the bed and threw it down. After an hour, she went out and gave Holofernes’ head to her maid.
And she put it into her food bag. The two of them went out together as they usually did, passed through the camp, went around through the valley, and climbed the mountain of Bethulia.

They came to the city gates, and Judith called from a distance to the gatekeepers, “Open, open the gates now, for the Lord our God is with us! May he again show his power in Israel and crush our enemies, just as he has done today!”
When the men of her city heard her voice, they hurried down to their city gates and summoned the priests and the elders of the people.
They gathered, from the least to the greatest, for they had been greatly astonished at her departure. They opened the city gate and brought them inside.
They lit their lamps and stood around them.
Judith said in a loud voice, “Children of Israel, bless God,
who has not withheld his mercy from the house of Israel, but has struck and driven back our enemies through my hand this very night!”

She took the head out of the bag, showed it to them, and said to them, “Here is the head of Holofernes, commander of the armies of Assyria, and here are the costly curtains beneath which he lay in his drunkenness. The Lord God has killed him by the hand of a woman.
As the Lord lives, he protected me along the way they traveled. The beauty of my face deceived him to his destruction, but he committed no defilement with me to bring shame upon me.”
All the people gave thanks, bowed down, and worshiped God. They all said with one voice, “Blessed are you, Lord our God, who today have put the enemies of your people to shame!
And Uzziah said to Judith, “Daughter, you are blessed by God Most High above all the women on earth.”
And blessed is the Lord God, who made heaven and earth, who gave you success against the head of that ruler, our enemy.

Your name will never fade from human memory, as people remember you before God forever. May the Lord my God exalt you and visit you with good things in return, because you did not spare yourself on account of our nation's suffering, but sought vengeance for the devastating blows we suffered, walking uprightly before our Lord.”
All the people said, “So be it! So be it!”
Judith said to them, “Listen, brothers, to what I tell you. Take this head and hang it in front of the battlements of the city walls.

When morning breaks and the sun rises over the earth, let all the men capable of fighting arm themselves. Appoint commanders over yourselves and go outside this city as though you were going down into the plain against one wing of the Assyrian slingers, but do not go down there.

Instead, throw them into confusion. They will take up their weapons and go into their main camp and rouse the commanders of Assyria. They will gather and make their way to Holofernes’ tent, but they will not find him.
Then terror will fall upon them, and they will turn and flee from you.”

Then you and all the inhabitants of the territory of Israel must follow them, strike them down, and pursue them along all their roads. But before doing this, summon Achior the Ammonite to me, so that he may see this man who trampled on the house of Israel, who bound him and had him brought here to die. They summoned Achior from Uzziah’s house. When he came and saw the head of Holofernes in the hand of a man from among the people, he fell on his face and rolled over. When he regained his strength, he fell at Judith’s feet, bowed before her, and said, “Blessed are you in all the settlements of Judah! Among all the nations, wherever they hear your name, they will be amazed. Now tell me how you accomplished this today.” Judith told him, before all her people, everything she had done from the day she went out until that moment. When Judith finished speaking, the people shouted loudly, glorifying God in their city.

When Achior saw all that the God of Israel had done, he believed in God with all his heart and was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin. He joined the house of Israel, where he remains to this day.

When morning dawned, they hung the head of Holofernes from the wall. Every man armed himself with his weapons, and they went out to do this through the passes along the mountainside. When the Assyrians saw them, they informed their leaders, who went to their commanders, officers, and captains of thousands.
They went to Holofernes’ tent and said to his chamberlain, “Go in now and wake our lord, for the slaves have dared to attack us in battle, so that we may destroy them completely.”
Bagoas went in and knocked on the door of the chamber, for he thought that Holofernes was asleep with Judith.

When no one answered him, he took courage and entered the chamber. He saw Holofernes lying naked on the ground, with his head removed from his body. Bagoas cried out loudly, weeping and lamenting bitterly, and tore his robe.
He entered Judith’s chamber and did not find her. Then he went out, ran to the troops, and said,
“The slaves have rebelled! A Hebrew woman has brought shame and disgrace upon the house of King Nebuchadnezzar. Look, Holofernes lies fallen on the ground, and his head is no longer on him!”
When the commanders of the Assyrian forces heard these words, they all tore their robes and were terribly afraid.
They cried out in the middle of the camp.
When those who were in the tents heard it, they were thrown into confusion because of what had happened.
Great fear and trembling fell upon them, and then no one remained beside his companion.
Scattered and confused, they all turned to flee into the plains and the hill country
around Bethulia, and from there they continued fleeing. Then all the fighting men of Israel attacked them.
Uzziah sent messengers to Betomesthaim, Choba, Kola, and all the territory of Israel with news of what had happened, so that everyone might gather together and pursue them to destroy them.

When the Israelites heard this, they all rushed together, fell upon them, and struck them down, slaughtering them as far as Choba. The people of Jerusalem did the same. All those who had come from the hill country told them what had happened in the camp. Those in Gilead and Galilee overtook them, struck them down, and drove them away until they had forced them past Damascus and its territory.

The other inhabitants of Bethulia went out and fell upon those occupying the Assyrian camp, plundering and gathering the spoils of the armies. Through these spoils the inhabitants of Bethulia became prosperous, had more than enough, and grew very wealthy.

The Israelites returned from the slaughter and began gathering the plunder and spoils of the fallen. People from the villages and farms in the hill country and the plains came and took what remained of the abundant spoils.
Joakim the high priest and the council of elders of the Israelites who lived in Jerusalem came to see the good things that the Lord God of Israel had done, and to see Judith and greet her with peace.
When they came in and saw her, they all blessed her together and said to her, “You are the glory of Jerusalem! You are the joy of Israel! You are the pride of our nation!
For with your own hands you have done all these good things for Israel, and God was pleased with them. May you be blessed by Almighty God forever!”
And all the people said, “So be it!”

The people carried away the spoils of the camp for thirty days. They gave Judith the tent of Holofernes, all the silver in the tent, the couches, and all his gold and silver utensils. She took them, loaded them onto her carts and pack animals, and brought them into the city.
All the women of Israel came to see her and blessed her, singing songs to her as they danced. She took branches of palm and olive trees, with their blossoms, and gave them to the women.

Other prominent women of the region also came in groups to praise her. All Israel followed them, armed and equipped, with wreaths of various colors on their heads and praises on everyone's lips to glorify God.
Judith began to sing this song of praise, and all Israel sang with her.
Judith said, “Sing to the Lord with drums and praise him with cymbals. Offer him songs and praises. Exalt him and call upon his name.
For the Lord God crushes wars.
And [?] his armies among the peoples, he saved me from the hands of my persecutors.
Assyria came from the mountains of the north, coming with tens of thousands of its troops. Their multitude covered the valleys, and the multitude of its horses covered the hills.
It declared that it would set fire to my territory, strike down my young men with the sword, carry off my children as plunder, and lead my virgins into captivity.
The Lord God Almighty overthrew them through the hand of a woman.

For their mighty warrior did not fall at the hands of young men; the sons of the Titans did not destroy him, nor did towering giants rise against him. Rather, Judith daughter of Merari utterly deceived him with the beauty of her face.
For she took off the clothing of her widowhood to raise up those who were oppressed in Israel.
She anointed her face with fragrant oils, adorned her head with her ornaments, and took her fine linen garment to deceive him.
The beauty of her sandaled feet led his heart astray, her beauty captivated his soul, and the dagger passed through his throat.
The Persians trembled at her boldness, and the Medes were thrown into confusion by her courage.
At that moment my afflicted ones cried out, and my sick ones shouted. They were overcome, raised their voices, and lost heart.
The sons of young women pierced them and slaughtered them like the children of destitute wanderers. They perished in the battle of my Lord.
I will praise the Lord my God with a new song of praise.
Lord, you are great and glorious, wondrous in your unfailing power.
Let all your creation serve you, for you spoke and they came into being; you sent your spirit, and they were created and formed. There is no one who resists your voice.

For the mountains were shaken from their foundations, together with the waters, and the rocks melted like wax before your face. But to those who fear you, you are forgiving. Every small sacrifice is a pleasing aroma, and the slightest bit of fat is a burnt offering to you.
But the one who is reverent is great forever.
Woe to those nations that have risen against our nation! The Lord Almighty will take vengeance on them on the day of judgment.
He will put fire and worms into their bodies, and they will weep in mourning forever.
When they went to Jerusalem, they worshiped God. Once the people had been purified, they brought their burnt offerings, their freewill offerings, and their sacrifices.
Judith brought out and dedicated all the furnishings and possessions of Holofernes, and gave them as offerings to the Lord God.
The people rejoiced in Jerusalem before the sanctuary for three months, and Judith remained with them.
After these days, they departed, each returning to their own inheritance. Judith went to Bethulia and took care of her household.
From that time onward, her name was honored throughout the whole land.
Many desired her throughout all the days of her life after Manasseh her husband died and was gathered to his people.

Judith grew greater and more honored day by day. She grew old there in her husband's house, reaching the age of one hundred and five years, and she freed her maidservant. She died in Bethulia, and they buried her in the tomb of Manasseh her husband.
The whole house of Israel mourned her for seven days. Before she died, she distributed her possessions to all the relatives of Manasseh her husband, and likewise to all her own relatives.
There was no one who terrified the children of Israel in the days of Judith or for many days after her death. End of Judith.
